title: Review of achievements and trends in graphene-based polymer nanocomposites for EMI shielding
abstract: Abstract The development of construction and smart buildings with increased application of various wireless communications has created a new form of pollution known as electromagnetic interference (EMI), which has resulted in a range of negative effects. To prevent such malfunctions, electronic devices must be shielded so that both incoming and outgoing interference are effectively filtered. This review presents an overview of the latest achievements and recent trends in the design and properties of graphene/polymer nanocomposites for EMI shielding. Two main groups are reviewed: (i) thermoplastic and (ii) thermoset polymer systems mixed with graphene, graphene oxide, and modified graphene, used to produce the corresponding nanocomposite films. In addition, graphene-foam-based nanocomposites are discussed as a distinct class of lightweight, three-dimensional architectures. The article emphasizes the relationships between composition, processing routes, microstructure, and shielding effectiveness across relevant frequency ranges, highlighting strategies to achieve high specific shielding performance at low filler loadings. This review intends to cover recent progress, current challenges, and future perspectives in the development of graphene/polymer nanocomposites as efficient EMI-shielding materials, providing a comprehensive overview of compositional, structural, and processing strategies for composites used in EMI-shielding applications.
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Electronics

sections.heading: Graphene
paragraphs: Graphene, as a two-dimensional carbon nanostructure, has attracted considerable interest as a new-generation solution for EMI shielding, due to graphene’s outstanding electrical conductivity, high specific surface area, and customizable structural morphology [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. These characteristics facilitate the formation of percolated conductive networks at relatively low filler loadings, thereby enhancing the reflection-dominated shielding commonly associated with highly conductive materials. However, excessive dependence on reflection is problematic due to potential secondary radiation, signal interference, and restricted bandwidth performance. In advanced technological sectors, such as stealth materials, next-generation electronics, and flexible or wearable devices, an overreliance on reflection is not optimal.

From its discovery in 2004, graphene has become one of the most attractive carbon-based nanostructures [ 1 ]. Graphene is the representative basic structural unit of all graphitic materials like fullerenes, graphite, and CNTs. The scientific community considers graphene as one of the world’s stiffest materials with enormous application potential in diverse sectors, ranging from the electrical industry, nanoelectronics, and environmental nanosensors to medicine, diagnostics, and even the fashion industry [ 1 ,  2 ]. Due to the  sp 2  hybridized carbon atoms in the monolayer graphene, it has a very low mass density compared to conventional fillers and possesses high electrical and thermal conductivity. It has been reported that the thermal conductivity of a monolayer graphene sheet has been determined to be extremely high, in the range of 4840 to 5300 W m −1  K −1  [ 3 ]. Besides its very efficient conductivity, graphene exhibits superior mechanical properties—it is estimated to be much stronger than steel, while remaining as flexible as rubber. Therefore, due to the superior electrical conductivity (higher than 10 7  S m −1 ), excellent mechanical properties (exceptional mechanical strength and flexibility), and high specific surface area (light and durable), graphene was intensively tested as an ideal nanofiller in graphene/polymer nanocomposites for efficient electromagnetic shielding applications. Graphene can very effectively dissipate absorbed electromagnetic radiation, reducing overheating risks and ensuring device reliability [ 4 ,  5 ]. In addition, besides its minimal thickness, graphene layers provide superior shielding performance, making it suitable for compact and lightweight devices. Based on these performances, graphene-based nanocomposite materials are able to be used for shielding against a wide spectrum of electromagnetic frequencies, meeting the various industrial and everyday consumer needs.

Critical factors that affect the EMI-shielding efficiency in graphene-based polymer nanocomposites include the amount, uniform graphene dispersion, and morphology of graphene and modified graphene nanostructures in polymer matrices [ 6 ,  7 ]. Additionally, the interface between the polymer matrix and graphene plays an important role in structuring an effective polymer/graphene system. It has been confirmed that a functionalized graphene surface resulted in strong physical or covalent interfacial interactions, which improve load transfer, network stability, and charge transport [ 8 ,  9 ]. Due to the synergy between the polymer matrix and graphene nanostructure, remarkable changes and enhancements in the physical properties of these nanocomposites have been reported. Interpenetrating networks can be developed in polymer/graphene nanomaterials, providing excellent electron mobility and improving electromagnetic protection behavior. Although challenges remain in cost, scalability, long-term stability, and the realization of ultra-thin, ultra-light designs, advances in hybrid fillers, novel architectures, and processing strategies are continually pushing the field forward.

This review aims to present an overview of the latest achievements and trends in the design and properties of graphene/polymer nanocomposites for EMI shielding. Based on the nature of the polymer matrix, two main groups are considered: (i) thermoplastic and (ii) thermoset polymer systems mixed with graphene, graphene oxide, and modified graphene, used for the production of the corresponding nanocomposite films. In addition, a separate group of graphene-foam-based nanocomposites is included [ 10 ], highlighting the potential of three-dimensional, lightweight architectures for high-performance EMI shielding across a broad frequency range.

sections.heading: EMI
paragraphs: Due to the rapid advances in telecommunications and increased wireless communication, the human population is increasingly exposed to various electromagnetic devices integrated into modern smart buildings. As a consequence, electromagnetic pollution has become a serious threat, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding has attracted great interest. EMI can negatively affect the communication, causing service interruption, data loss, permanent damage to equipment, and system failure. In practice, EMI shielding is achieved by minimizing the signal that passes through a system via surface reflections and/or absorption of the radiated power.

EMI-shielding materials contain mobile charge carriers and/or polarization mechanisms that limit the transmission of electromagnetic waves. Traditionally, metals have been widely used as EMI-shielding materials because they are excellent electrical conductors and strongly reflect EM waves. However, they suffer from significant drawbacks, including high weight and density, lack of flexibility, corrosion susceptibility, and processing difficulties, which restrict their application in lightweight and flexible electronics. With the development of new polymer-based composite materials filled with various conductive nanostructures, most of these disadvantages can be overcome.

Polymer nanocomposites filled with graphene are particularly attractive alternatives because they exhibit a unique combination of electrical, thermal, dielectric, magnetic, and mechanical properties. In this context, the main challenges are related to the proper processing of graphene to obtain a uniform dispersion within the polymer matrix, while minimizing agglomeration or restacking of graphene sheets and ensuring good percolation at low loadings. Current research trends focus on the design and development of thin, lightweight, highly flexible, next-generation smart materials capable of absorbing strong EM radiation over a wide frequency range [ 11 ,  12 ]. Based on the market analyses, Orasugh and Ray reported that there is a remarkable increase in demand for new, more effective EMI-shielding materials. This demand reflected in a sharp increase in publications on Science Direct for “Effective electromagnetic interference shielding materials” that were published over the last two decades, such as 780 in 2019, 951 in 2020, and 1016 in 2021 [ 13 ]. According to electromagnetic theory, EMI-shielding effectiveness (SE) is defined as the primary metric used to evaluate the performance of a shielding material and quantifies the attenuation of an incident EM wave by the shield. When electromagnetic waves encounter the surface of a shielding material, electromagnetic radiation can be attenuated through three mechanisms: Reflection ( R ) at the surface, Absorption ( A ) within the bulk of the material, and multiple reflections (MR) inside the shield, as shown in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Electromagnetic shielding mechanism diagram of graphene-based materials

Effective EMI-shielding materials require high electrical conductivity to efficiently reflect electromagnetic radiation, because mobile charge carriers interact directly with the incident EM fields. Absorption, on the other hand, arises when the radiation interacts with electric or magnetic dipoles in the shielding medium, while scattering and impedance mismatches at internal interfaces contribute to multiple reflections. SE can be determined theoretically by solving Maxwell’s equations analytically or numerically using bulk material properties such as conductivity, permittivity, and permeability, or it can be measured experimentally and approximated from the known properties of the composite constituents. In this review, the main EMI-shielding aspects for each type of graphene/polymer nanocomposite system are analyzed in separate sections devoted to thermoplastic matrices, thermoset matrices, and graphene-foam-based systems, highlighting composition–structure–property relationships and application-relevant performance (Fig.  2 ). Fig. 2 Composition–structure–property relationships and EMI-shielding mechanism of polymer/graphene nanocomposites

sections.heading: Thermoplastic polymer/graphene nanocomposites for EMI shielding
paragraphs: The development of thermoplastic polymer nanocomposites incorporating graphene (or its derivatives) has emerged as a promising approach for lightweight and easy-to-process EMI-shielding materials. Compared to traditional metal-based shields, these composites offer recyclability, easier fabrication (e.g., melt blending, extrusion), and greater design flexibility. By optimizing matrix composition, filler type and loading, architecture (foams, layered stacks, orientation), and processing methods, significant shielding effectiveness can be achieved (typically in the tens of dB range in the X-band), with some systems reaching even higher values (e.g., hundreds of dB cm −1  specific measure). This section highlights key aspects in thermoplastic polymer/graphene nanocomposites systems, such as matrix-filler selection, network formation and percolation, composite architecture and processing, EMI-shielding performance, and future directions.

sections.heading: Matrix-filler selection and graphene integration
paragraphs: In thermoplastic systems, the choice of matrix material largely determines mechanical performance, thermal stability, processability, and suitability for specific service environments, while graphene-based nanofillers primarily serve to establish electrically conductive and/or electromagnetic-active networks. Commonly studied thermoplastic matrices include, for instance, thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), polypropylene (PP), and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), each offering distinct mechanical flexibility, chemical resistance, and ease of processing [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. The compatibility between the chosen polymer and graphene derivatives strongly influences filler dispersion, interfacial adhesion, and ultimately composite performance.

The incorporation of graphene and its derivatives, such as graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) or reduced graphene oxide (rGO), into thermoplastic matrices allows the formation of continuous conductive pathways at relatively low loadings, often significantly lower than conventional conductive fillers like carbon black or metal powders [ 6 ]. For example, Verma  et al.  reported TPU/graphene nanocomposites with loadings of 0–5.5 vol.%, achieving notable EMI shielding in the X-band (8.2–12.4 GHz) [ 17 ]. Other studies show that even 1–3 wt% graphene derivatives in microcellular foams can produce substantial shielding due to the combined effects of conductive networks and multiple internal reflections [ 18 ]. Despite these advantages, achieving uniform dispersion, minimizing agglomeration, and promoting strong interfacial adhesion remain key challenges. The polymer-graphene interfacial region plays a critical role: enhanced interfacial interactions improve electron transport, network connectivity, and dielectric loss mechanisms, directly contributing to EMI-shielding efficiency. Strategies to improve the polymer/graphene interface include surface functionalization of graphene, compatibilizers, ultrasonication-assisted mixing, and in situ polymerization, which promote better filler wetting, reduce voids, and stabilize the conductive network. Moreover, the matrix-filler combination influences thermal, mechanical, and processing characteristics, allowing the design of multifunctional materials. For instance, flexible matrices such as TPU enable lightweight and wearable shielding solutions, while more rigid matrices like PMMA or PP can enhance structural stability at the cost of reduced flexibility [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ]. A concise overview of commonly used thermoplastic matrices and their possible effects on EMI shielding is shown in Table  1 . Table 1 Typical thermoplastic matrices for EMI-shielding purposes Matrix Typical properties Effect on EMI shielding TPU Flexible, elastic, thermally stable Good network formation at low loadings; high flexibility LLDPE Lightweight, chemically resistant Effective at low loadings in foamed or layered structures HDPE Rigid, chemically resistant PP Rigid, good thermal stability Moderate shielding, higher loading needed PMMA Transparent, stiff Moderate shielding, limited flexibility

Through careful matrix-filler selection, filler functionalization, and processing optimization, thermoplastic/graphene nanocomposites can be tailored to achieve high EMI shielding, mechanical integrity, and multifunctionality, supporting applications across aerospace, automotive, telecommunications, and wearable devices.

sections.heading: Network formation, percolation, and composite structure
paragraphs: The EMI-shielding performance of graphene-thermoplastic nanocomposites is closely linked to the formation of an effective filler network (i.e., percolation threshold) and the distribution of graphene within the matrix. Once the filler content crosses a critical percolation threshold, the composite becomes conductive and can reflect and absorb electromagnetic waves. For instance, several reviews emphasize that dispersion, filler aspect ratio, orientation, and matrix-filler interfacial interaction are key factors controlling network formation and therefore EMI-shielding performance. In thermoplastic graphene composites, important parameters include graphene loading, aspect ratio/flake size, orientation, and architecture (e.g., layered films, foam/porous structures, aligned networks). For example, a work on foam composites of HDPE with GNPs prepared via supercritical-fluid treatment and foaming reported a substantial drop in percolation threshold and increased through-plane conductivity: the composite foams had a percolation threshold reduced by up to ~ 62% compared to solid counterparts, and achieved a K-band EMI SE of ~ 31.6 dB at ~ 9.8 vol.% GNP [ 22 ]. Another study on TPU composites with GNPs prepared via supercritical CO 2  foaming reported an electrical conductivity of ~ 2.77 S m −1  and EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) of ~ 24.7 dB at just 3.71 vol.% loading in the X‐band [ 23 ].

Orientation and architecture play major roles: Xu et al. fabricated oriented graphene fiber film (GFF)/polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) laminates (though PDMS is elastomeric, not strictly thermoplastic) where fiber orientation relative to the electric field component altered SE by up to 32 dB at ~ 8.8 GHz. The optimal two-ply unidirectional laminate achieved ~ 50.6 dB [ 24 ]. In thermoplastic nanocomposites, foam structures (microcellular foams) can increase the multiple-scattering and absorption pathways of incident electromagnetic waves, enhancing shielding by absorption rather than pure reflection. One TPU/GNP foam study reported comparable specific SE at much lower graphene content (1 wt%) than conventional systems [ 25 ].

sections.heading: Processing, composite architecture, and effects on performance
paragraphs: The processing of thermoplastic graphene nanocomposites plays a decisive role in defining their microstructure and, consequently, their EMI-shielding behavior. Common processing techniques include melt blending, solution blending, compression molding, extrusion, and foam expansion. Each of these methods imposes distinct thermal and shear conditions on the material, influencing the dispersion of graphene within the polymer matrix, the orientation of the flakes, and the possible formation of voids or cellular structures. These microstructural factors, in turn, determine how efficiently a percolated conductive network forms and how effectively the composite interacts with and attenuates electromagnetic radiation.

In melt blending, the polymer and filler are mixed in the molten state, and the resulting dispersion largely depends on parameters such as viscosity, shear rate, and the interfacial affinity between graphene and the polymer chains. Good dispersion promotes network continuity, lowering the percolation threshold and enhancing conductivity, whereas poor dispersion or agglomeration disrupts the conductive paths, increasing the threshold and reducing EMI shielding effectiveness. Solution blending, on the other hand, involves dispersing graphene in a solvent before mixing with a polymer solution, allowing better exfoliation and distribution of the nanofiller. However, the solvent removal step can sometimes induce re-agglomeration or residual porosity, which affects the homogeneity of the conductive network. Compression molding and extrusion impose flow fields that can partially align graphene flakes along specific directions, giving rise to anisotropic electrical and shielding properties. Foam-expansion techniques, including supercritical CO 2  foaming, introduce a cellular morphology that promotes multiple internal reflections and scattering of incident electromagnetic waves. The presence of pores can also reduce material density and favor shielding by absorption rather than by pure reflection, which is desirable for lightweight and flexible devices [ 26 ].

TPU/graphene systems fabricated through both melt mixing and solution blending hold strong potential for synergistically improving shielding performance through complementary conductive and magnetic losses5. Building on this concept, Wilson et al. developed a multilayer thermoplastic polyurethane system containing alternating layers of graphite-filled TPU (G-TPU) and spinel ferrite nanoparticle-filled TPU (F-TPU). Each layer was approximately 0.8 mm thick, and different stacking sequences were tested in the X-band (8.2–12.4 GHz). The purely ferrite-filled configuration achieved an EMI SE of around 3.7 dB, the fully graphite-filled one reached 33.8 dB, while the hybrid F/G/F and G/F/G stacks reached 23.9 and 54.0 dB, respectively. The dramatic enhancement observed for the G/F/G configuration clearly demonstrates that the internal architecture, and specifically the sequence of conductive and magnetic layers, governs the balance between reflection, absorption, and multiple-scattering of electromagnetic waves [ 27 ].

Other studies have similarly shown how controlling processing and architecture can tune shielding efficiency. For instance, TPU/graphene nanoplatelet foams prepared via microcellular foaming exhibited comparable specific EMI shielding effectiveness to dense composites, despite containing only 1 wt% graphene. The foam structure enhanced absorption mechanisms due to the extended path length and multiple internal reflections across the cell walls [ 25 ].

Taken together, these results confirm that processing strategy and resulting architecture, encompassing the dispersion and orientation of graphene, the presence of pores or layers, the combination of conductive and magnetic fillers, and the thickness of individual layers, are key factors in determining the EMI-shielding efficiency of thermoplastic graphene nanocomposites. Tailoring these parameters enables the rational design of multifunctional, lightweight, and high-performance materials suitable for modern electromagnetic protection applications.

sections.heading: EMI-shielding performance of thermoplastic graphene nanocomposites
paragraphs: Although thermoplastic composites incorporating graphene have achieved significant improvements in electrical conductivity and EMI shielding compared to unfilled polymers, their overall SE values still tend to be somewhat lower than those of dense metal or ceramic/metal-based systems, which typically rely on high reflectivity rather than absorption mechanisms. Nevertheless, the progress in thermoplastic–graphene systems is noteworthy, particularly because these materials combine lightweight character, flexibility, and processability with tunable electromagnetic performance [ 19 ,  26 ].

In the case of TPU, an EMI SE of approximately 21 dB at 5.5 vol.% graphene content in the X-band (8.2–12.4 GHz) was observed, and it is already sufficient for moderate shielding applications such as wearable or flexible electronics [ 27 ]. Similarly, rGO dispersed within TPU via solution blending has achieved up to 53 dB at 2.5 wt% loading, reflecting the critical role of uniform dispersion and interfacial compatibility in establishing a continuous conductive pathway [ 28 ]. In LLDPE matrices filled with 5 wt% of graphene derivatives, shielding effectiveness values of –21 dB, –17 dB, and –19 dB were observed in different configurations and orientations, illustrating how subtle differences in composite morphology or filler alignment can produce measurable variations in shielding response [ 29 ]. Even more striking performance has been reported in PP systems, where a nanocomposite based on recycled mask fibers blended with graphene nanoplatelets (PP@G) achieved a maximum SE of 88 dB (or 1100 dB cm −1  when normalized by thickness), demonstrating that, under optimized processing and network formation, thermoplastic–graphene composites can rival or even surpass some metal-based materials in shielding efficiency [ 30 ,  31 ].

Comparable advances have also been achieved through structural design rather than simple filler addition. The cellular morphology introduced by foaming increased the number of internal reflections and scattering events, thereby enhancing absorption without significantly increasing density [ 25 ]. These results collectively demonstrate that specific shielding performance, measured as EMI SE per unit thickness or mass, can reach or exceed 40 dB even at low filler loadings when the architecture is properly optimized. Such efficiency makes thermoplastic graphene nanocomposites particularly appealing for lightweight and flexible EMI-shielding applications, such as portable electronics, sensors, and soft robotic systems.

Mechanistically, shielding in these materials arises from the interplay of reflection, absorption, and multiple internal reflections. The reflection component is primarily governed by the mobile charge carriers within the percolated graphene network, which generate impedance mismatch at the air–composite interface. Absorption, in contrast, depends on dielectric and magnetic losses, interfacial polarization, and the multiple-scattering of electromagnetic waves within the heterogeneous composite microstructure. Graphene’s high intrinsic conductivity promotes reflection, but it is the network topology, including flake orientation, interflake junctions, voids, and interfaces, that enhances absorption. Improved interfacial coupling between graphene and the thermoplastic matrix also contributes to polarization losses and dipole relaxation, further strengthening the absorption component of EMI shielding [ 26 ]. Consequently, modern research increasingly emphasizes the design of absorption-dominant rather than purely reflective shielding materials, as the former minimize secondary electromagnetic pollution and yield more stable, broadband attenuation profiles.

sections.heading: Thermosetting polymer/graphene nanocomposites
paragraphs: One of the most designed and modified G/thermosetting polymer systems is based on the curing epoxy matrix, still attractive due to the wide variations in the manufacturing and synthesis process, which involves a sequential curing stage, attractive fillers and other constituents, selective and fast methodology [ 32 ]. Graphene’s nanostructures exhibit high surface energy, which leads to a strong tendency of agglomeration, and because of that, a high shear mixing is selected as a good tool for the de-aggregation and well dispersion of nanofillers into thermosetting resins. Epoxy-based graphene composites were first reported in 2007 by Yu and his team [ 33 ]. They used a multistep approach, including acid intercalation, thermal exfoliation, physical separation, and dispersion to transform the natural graphite into few-layer graphene plates. A high shear mixing approach was then applied to achieve a homogeneous graphene dispersion in the epoxy matrix. The obtained composites exhibited better thermal conductivities (up to 1.45 W m K −1  at low-volume graphene loadings (≈5 vol.%)) compared to other carbon nanostructures [ 33 ]. Collado et al. worked on the thiol epoxy/graphene nanostructures. They found out that the thiol–epoxy chemistry provides the synthesis of an epoxy system with high shape-memory capabilities. In this way, dual-curing epoxy systems reinforced with graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) were manufactured. They studied the influence of the GNs content, which greatly increases upon loading while retaining a high shape-memory fixation and recovery rates (near 99%). A maximum EMI shielding efficiency of 24 dB was achieved for the higher GNPs content [ 32 ]. Besides the high shear mixing, another dispersion method commonly used for the production of graphene/epoxy nanocomposites was sonication. Although the obtained nanocomposites exhibited enhanced mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties, this process was not proven to be scalable. Ghaleb et al. [ 34 ] studied the effect of sonication time and filler loading using both graphene nano-powder and carbon nanotubes dispersed in epoxy. A maximum electrical conductivity of roughly 10 −2  S/m was found after only 20 min and 1 vol.% of graphene filler. It was also reported that although higher sonication times lead to more homogenous dispersions with fewer agglomerations, damage to the graphene nanostructure was apparent at these higher sonication times. Another precondition for the production of graphene/epoxy nanocomposites with good SE was to create an aligned structure of graphene filler throughout the polymer matrix. The obtained nanocomposites demonstrated superior properties such as highly anisotropic behavior, liquid crystallinity, and low percolation thresholds [ 34 ]. Yousefi et al .  worked on dispersion of rGO in an epoxy polymer matrix in an aligned manner, which resulted in a nanocomposite with an SE of 38 dB and a high dielectric constant of greater than 1400 at 3 wt% of rGO [ 35 ]. The measured high dielectric constant was attributed to charge accumulation at the filler–matrix interface due to the Maxwell–Wagner–Sillars effect. In another paper, it was shown that a proper graphene structure alignment through the epoxy matrix was obtained using the external electrical field during the curing process [ 36 ]. Namely, Wu et al. studied the graphene flakes alignment throughout an epoxy matrix using the application of an external electrical field, and they reported that the obtained nanocomposites exhibited excellent thermal, mechanical, and electrical properties. An increase of 60% in thermal conductivity and 900% increase in fracture toughness of the nanocomposites are compared to that of the pure epoxy. Electrical conductivity was increased to a 7–8 order of magnitude [ 36 ]. The fabrication process involved sonicating the graphene and liquid resin, followed by calendaring. An alternating electric field was applied during the curing process of the fabricated sample provided by a signal generator and a wideband amplifier. The electrical conductivity was reported to be roughly two orders of magnitude higher in the direction parallel to the alignment than in the direction perpendicular to the alignment. Abdelal and his team [ 37 ] have studied the EMI-shielding properties of graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs)/epoxy composites filled with a wide range of filler concentrations (1–17 wt%). They also tested GNPs with three different surface areas (300, 500, and 700 m 2  g −1 ). By measuring electromagnetic properties, they have modeled the SE of graphene/epoxy NC. The obtained results confirmed that the dielectric constant and EMI SE were highly dependent on the GNPs’ surface area and content. The best EMI-shielding performance was measured for the GNPs/epoxy with 17 wt%. A similar analysis was done by Liang et al. [ 38 ], who produced epoxy/graphene nanocomposites with graphene content from 0.1 to 15 wt%. These nanocomposite sheets demonstrated a low percolation threshold (0.52 vol.%) that exhibited SE of 21 dB (15 wt%). Wan et al. published a study related to the EMI-shielding performances of 3D graphene aerogel-–epoxy (GA-EP) composites [ 39 ]. They used an infiltration method to produce GA-EP composites using porous graphene with a controllable cellular structure. Graphene aerogel with different pore sizes and morphologies was obtained from graphene oxide precursors of different sizes. They reported the results of the EMI-shielding performance and mechanical properties, as well as the thermal stability of GA–EP composites. Namely, it was confirmed GA–EP composite possesses superior EMI properties and compressive strength (GA–EP with a thickness of 3 mm and 1.0 wt% graphene filler exhibits an EMI shielding effectiveness of around 30 dB in the measured frequency range of 10–20 GHz and compressive strength of 56.01 ± 1.57 MPa). The obtained results suggest that the macro-properties, including EMI shielding, conductivity, and mechanical properties of GA–polymer composites, can be designed based on the GO precursor sheets with different sizes. These graphene aerogel–epoxy composites with excellent EMI performance demonstrate very high potential applications in various fields such as electronics, automobiles, and aircraft [ 39 ].

Madinhel and his team studied the EMI-shielding performances of the graphene/polyester nanocomposites [ 40 ]. They tested the effects of the size and concentration of graphene nanostructures, as well as the processing method, on the electrical conductivity and electromagnetic behavior of the nanocomposites fabricated by compression molding. They found out that the graphene orientation in the obtained composite is not affected by the compression process, and consequently, the electrical conductivity of these nanocomposites demonstrates only a slight anisotropy. Measurements of the cross-plane conductivity of pure polyester and graphene/PES composite with 5 wt% graphene NSs content were determined to be 9 × 10 15  S cm −1  and 1.4 × 10 14  S cm −1 , respectively. Theoretically, at low concentrations, conductivity is measured due to the electron tunneling, which occurs through the matrix/filler interfaces. PES is an insulator because the bound charges of the polyester belong to the valence band. Increasing the graphene fraction in the matrix, the fillers get closer together, and at a critical concentration range called the percolation threshold, the first conductive networks form. The conductivity determined for the nanocomposite loaded with 7.5 wt% G NSs significantly increased to 6 × 10 7  S cm −1 . The maximum EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) of 27 dB was measured at 25 wt% of the graphene loading.

sections.heading: Graphene-polymer foams
paragraphs: Graphene-polymer foams received great attention in the design and development of proper EMI-shielding materials due to their advantages, such as lightweight and the unique porous structure that effectively absorbs EM waves. Theoretically, graphene-foam nanocomposites exhibited absorption-dominated shielding phenomena, which meet the present standards of EMI-shielding applications. According to practical experience, it was confirmed that EMI shielding efficiency could be enhanced by designing and creating heterogeneous materials due to the scattering at the interface between materials in the multiple reflection mechanism. The pores developed in the lightweight 3D structure decrease the density of the material and are also supposed to increase multiple internal reflections of EM waves, increasing EMISE values. Porosity has been integrated into the material to reduce the density of the EMI-shielding materials to get the best of both SE and lightweight, and the impact of porosity on the properties and structure of porous materials has been adequately studied. In fact, it was confirmed that the foaming of graphene films improves its EMI shielding efficiency (EMI SE) due to multiple internal reflections by microcellular structures [ 10 ,  41 ]. By introducing the cellular structures into graphene–polymer nanocomposites, the obtained foam structures enriched the graphene within or on the cell walls and resulted in the electrically conductive networks above the percolation threshold. The obtained graphene-polymer nanocomposite foams exhibited abundant micropores surrounded by a conducting frame, which demonstrates a higher EMI-shielding efficiency. The created porous architectures of the foams can reflect and scatter the incident electromagnetic waves many times between the cell walls, and open or closed cells can eventually absorb microwaves after multiple reflections. Due to the foam morphology, graphene foams exhibit excellent EMI SE values at lower weights and smaller thicknesses than non-foamed composites [ 42 ]. According to the literature review, there are three different routes to produce graphene–polymer nanocomposite foams, shown in Fig.  3 . [ 43 ] .  Namely, Sun and Zhou reported the following routes: (i) polymer foams that are coated with graphene nanosheets; (ii) graphene foams that are coated with polymer layers; and (iii) graphene dispersed within the skeleton of the polymeric foam. Additionally, it was confirmed that the properties of the graphene’s foam nanocomposites depend on the method used for their production, such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD), 3D printing, self-assembly of graphene oxide–freeze-drying, hydrothermal, dip-coating, and supercritical CO 2  forming. [ 42 ]. Commercially, on the market, available are graphene-based free-standing foams produced from polyurethane (PU) and melamine foams aimed to be tested for EMI-shielding protection [ 44 ]. Namely, Li et al. published a production method in which commercial melamine resin was primarily carbonized in a furnace at temperatures from 300 to 800 °C, and the obtained carbon structure was then coated with GO. Further, a vacuum-impregnation process was used to create a graphene/epoxy foam. The obtained graphene/epoxy foam exhibited improved thermal and electrical conductivities of epoxy composites were significantly increased to 0.92 W m −1  K −1  and 0.70 S cm −1 , which were 318% and 13 orders of magnitude higher compared to that of pure epoxy [ 44 ]. Fig. 3 Synthesis methods of graphene-polymer composite foams

Xia et al .  worked with commercial polyurethane (PU) foam to create polymer-based graphene foams, using the process of immersing the PU foam into an aqueous solution of graphene oxide (GO). In this way, the hydrophobic graphene nanosheets were formed on the PU surface. The researchers observed a color change in the graphene foams after the pyrolysis of PU, indicating the successful formation of a continuous layer of graphene in a straightforward manner [ 45 ].

Shen et al. easily produced lightweight graphene–PU foams by dip-coating commercial PU sponges into a graphene oxide aqueous suspension, followed by the hydrothermal reduction of coated GO in the presence of hydrazine monohydrate [ 46 ]. The obtained graphene-PU foams had a low density of 0.027–0.030 g cm −3 . They exhibited high EMI shielding efficiency, which was determined by an absorption-dominant mechanism, conductive dissipation, multiple reflections, and the scattering of EM waves by the conductive graphene network.

Lin and coworkers worked on the method for foam production by using a dip-coating method to fabricate graphene/PU foams coated with Ni-rGO. They used nickel sulfate in a GO aqueous suspension during this process [ 47 ]. This method resulted in the creation of rGO and Ni nanoparticles on the surface of the PU foam. The obtained Ni-rGO-coated PU foams, with a thickness of 10 mm, demonstrated excellent electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness (EMI SE) of 24.03–27.71 dB in the frequency range of 30–1500 MHz. These foams accomplished the practical requirements, keeping the primary compressibility of the PU foams.

Yan et al. developed and applied a new two-step method based on high-pressure compression molding and salt leaching to produce graphene–polystyrene (GPS) foam nanocomposites [ 48 ]. They produced two foam samples with the same graphene content of 30 wt%, but with various porosities and densities, labeled GPS045 of 0.45 g cm −3  (60% porosity) and GPS027 of 0.27 g cm −3  (76% porosity). The results of conductivity measurements show that the sample GPS045 (1.25 S m −1 ) was higher than that of GPS027 (0.22 S m −1 ). The EMI SE results show that the total of GPS045 was higher than that of GPS027 over the whole frequency range. The average SE total of GPS045 was approximately 29.3 dB, while that of GPS027 was 17.3 dB for 2.5-mm-thick samples. The obtained results suggested that better conductivity contributes more to the shielding performance than higher porosity [ 48 ].

Jiatong Li and coworkers published the research work on PVA nanocomposites with 7 graphene layers [ 49 ]. In fact, they were inspired by the structure of multilayer steamed bread, and they designed a new alternating multilayered structure with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-derived graphene/electrospun carbon nanofibers layers applying the alternating vacuum-assisted filtration method. They used GO/aPAN nanofibers as a solution and PVA aerogel film matrix in order to composite an alternating film by scraping and coating. In the second phase, they prepared the multilayer porous alternating graphene-based film by using high-temperature annealing reduction. As a result, they obtained the multilayer structure composed of PVA and GO/aPAN nanofibers, which was additionally thermally treated at high temperature in order to increase the multiple reflection absorption of electromagnetic waves. Their EMI-shielding testing in the range of 8–12 GHz resulted in the EMI-shielding value increasing from 32 to 80 dB, and the shielding efficiency increased from 99.87 to 99.99%.

Jingnan Ni et al. published the work on testing of EMI shielding efficiency of graphene aerogel/ polydimethylsiloxane metacomposites with tunable electrical conductivity [ 50 ]. In order to satisfy the demand for multiple performances in the electromagnetic field, multi-interfaced graphene aerogel (GA)/polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composites with an integral three-dimensional (3-D) structure were constructed. In the microwave frequency range (1 MHz–1 GHz), the GA/PDMS composites exhibited negative permittivity corresponding to the plasmonic state at low frequencies, which resulted from efficacious multiple interfaces in the GA/PDMS composites. It was determined that the negative permittivity could be adjusted by changing the testing pressure and the GA amount. Multiple interfaces belonging to the GA were beneficial to achieve microwave absorption and EMI shielding. A much wider microwave absorption bandwidth, i.e., 9.15 GHz, was observed and was increased by more than 2–3 times compared with similar research, together with a total shielding effectiveness (SET) of over 60 dB from 2 to 18 GHz. The multifunctional GA/PDMS composites have the potential to be an effective electromagnetic protection material.

This comparison highlights the critical influence of the polymer matrix, filler architecture (from 2D films to 3D foams), and processing techniques on the resulting shielding effectiveness.
