Notably, while absolute EMI SE values are frequently reported, the transition toward lightweight and porous structures, such as those described in Sect.  5 , emphasizes the importance of normalized shielding effectiveness (SE divided by thickness or density) to accurately benchmark material efficiency. Furthermore, the data indicate a clear trend: while reflection remains a significant component due to graphene’s high conductivity, the development of sophisticated foam architectures and hybrid filler systems is increasingly shifting the dominant attenuation mechanism toward absorption. This shift is essential for the next generation of smart building materials aimed at reducing secondary electromagnetic pollution.

sections.heading: Dielectric or magnetic additives-graphene-based polymer nanocomposites
paragraphs: To enhance the absorption performance of the shielding mechanism and to broaden its effective operating bandwidth, current research efforts are directed toward the modification of graphene through the integration of various nanomaterials that introduce additional loss mechanisms. This enhancement is primarily achieved by the incorporation of dielectric and/or magnetic nanoparticles.

In this section, a clearer comparative evaluation is established by categorizing electromagnetic performance metrics into unified, cross-system parameters to ensure a robust benchmarking framework. Consequently, two distinct classes of electromagnetic performance metrics are carefully considered to avoid common evaluation pitfalls. Shielding effectiveness (SE) refers to the attenuation of transmitted fields through a material or enclosure and is defined as the ratio (in dB) of the field strength without the shield to that with the shield, integrating reflection, absorption, and multiple reflection contributions. By contrast, radar-absorbing metrics such as reflection loss (RL) and effective absorption bandwidth describe how much of an incident wave is absorbed by a coating or laminate under matched-impedance conditions; RL is the logarithmic ratio (in dB) of reflected to incident power at a single interface, and the effective bandwidth is usually defined as the frequency range where RL is below a given threshold (often − 10 dB, corresponding to approximately 90% absorption). In what follows, SE values are discussed in the context of enclosure-type shielding and transmission attenuation, whereas RL and absorption bandwidth are used strictly for radar-absorbing and coating-type configurations, as summarized in Table  3 . Table 3 Summary of electromagnetic performance metrics and their use in this section Metric Symbol Typical configuration Physical meaning (qualitative) Shielding effectiveness SE, SE T Enclosure / bulk shields, transmission tests Logarithmic attenuation (in dB) of the field transmitted through the shield (incident vs transmitted) Absorption shielding effectiveness SE A Decomposition of SE Portion of SE attributed to absorption of EM energy inside the material Reflection shielding effectiveness SE R Decomposition of SE Portion of SE attributed to reflection at the incident interface Reflection loss (absorber) RL Radar‑absorbing layers, coatings (RAM) Logarithmic measure (in dB) of the power reflected from the absorber surface relative to the incident power Effective absorption bandwidth – Radar‑absorbing layers, coatings (RAM) Frequency range over which RL is below a specified threshold (commonly − 10 dB, i.e., ≥ 90% absorption)

The integration of dielectric materials into graphene matrices has emerged as an effective strategy to extend loss mechanisms beyond conduction alone. Dielectric compounds, including titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ), barium titanate (BaTiO 3 ), nickel oxide (NiO), aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3 ), silicon carbide (SiC), and various perovskite-structured particles, can introduce interfacial polarization, dipole relaxation, and space-charge accumulation [ 51 ,  52 – 53 ]. The formation of nanoscale heterojunctions between graphene layers and dielectric fillers facilitates Maxwell–Wagner–Sillars (MWS) polarization [ 54 ], thereby enhancing dielectric loss within the microwave frequency range. Furthermore, these dielectric fillers disrupt the continuity of graphene’s conductive network, resulting in increased internal scattering and improved impedance matching—critical factors for maximizing absorption while minimizing specular reflection. The optimization of dielectric filler content is paramount. An inadequate loading leads to diminished polarization effects, whereas excessive incorporation may compromise the conductive pathways essential for the reflection component of shielding effectiveness. As evidenced in various studies [ 55 ,  56 ,  57 – 58 ], appropriately engineered graphene–dielectric composites can achieve broadband absorption at reduced overall thicknesses while also demonstrating enhanced thermal and chemical stability in comparison to pristine graphene.
A significant body of research investigates a range of nanostructures and dielectric material compositions aimed at enhancing the EMI shielding effectiveness of graphene-based composites.

Tong et al. [ 59 ] developed high-performance electromagnetic wave (EMW) absorbing materials, based on three-dimensional hierarchical reduced graphene oxide (rGO) aerogel framework incorporating TiO 2 /Ti 3 C 2 T x  hybrid structures, synthesized through a hydrothermal process followed by a mild chemical reduction step. At a filler loading of 10 wt%, the aerogel exhibits a maximum reflection loss (RL) of 65.3 dB at an optimal matching thickness of 2.5 mm, indicating highly efficient radar-wave absorption at that frequency. Moreover, an effective absorption bandwidth (defined as RL <  − 10 dB, i.e., ≥ 90% absorption of the incident power) of 4.3 GHz is achieved with a coating thickness of only 2.0 mm. The absorption bandwidth can be further tuned up to 13.74 GHz by adjusting the absorber thickness between 1.5 and 5.0 mm. The superior EMW absorption capability arises from the highly porous conductive architecture, enhanced impedance matching, multiple internal reflections and scattering events, and defect-induced polarization mechanisms. Overall, these findings demonstrate a viable strategy for producing lightweight, thin, and broadband electromagnetic wave absorbers rather than enclosure-type shields, suitable for applications requiring minimization of specular reflection and radar cross-section.

The research conducted by Kumar et al. [ 56 ] focused on developing a composite material with mechanical strength, anticorrosive properties, and EMI-shielding capabilities. This material uses epoxy as the matrix and incorporates graphene as a conductive filler and TiO 2  as a dielectric filler. The nanocomposites were prepared using an ultrasonic mixing process. The graphene/TiO2–epoxy nanocomposite (epoxy + 0.25 wt% graphene + 0.25 wt% TiO 2 ) exhibited exceptional anticorrosion properties, achieving a maximum corrosion protection level of 99.96%. Furthermore, it demonstrated a total shielding effectiveness in transmission (SET) of − 11 dB, which translates to over 90% attenuation of the transmitted signal in the tested configuration, in contrast to neat epoxy, which displayed a SET of approximately − 3 dB (≈50% attenuation). Additionally, the graphene/TiO 2 –epoxy nanocomposite showed significant enhancements, with increases of about 36% in tensile strength and 84% in storage modulus compared to the neat epoxy.

Tong et al. [ 60 ] explored the synergistic interactions among constituents in multi-component composites, significantly enhancing EMI shielding effectiveness. In their study, microwave-reduced graphene aerogel (MRGA) functions as a three-dimensional network scaffold, onto which TiO 2  is generated in situ using a sol–gel method, followed by a microwave-assisted reduction. The TiO 2 /MRGA is subsequently embedded in epoxy resin and cured to create the composite. The presence of Ti–O–C bonds confirms the effective integration between TiO 2  and MRGA. Under electromagnetic irradiation, the combination of MRGA and TiO 2  produces a synergistic effect, leading to enhanced EMI shielding effectiveness. At a mass ratio of TiO 2  to MRGA of 1.5:1, the composite achieves a maximum EMI shielding effectiveness in transmission of 32.5 dB in the X-band, corresponding to a reduction of the transmitted field by approximately three orders of magnitude. Furthermore, when the TiO 2  to MRGA ratio ranges from 1 to 1.8, the average EMI shielding effectiveness of the composites increases by 37% compared to that of MRGA/epoxy composites. These findings underscore the considerable potential of this type of EMI-shielding material for various applications.

Araujo et al. [ 61 ] directed their research on the influence of TiO 2  in polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) films reinforced with either graphene oxide (GO) or reduced graphene oxide (rGO), with a particular focus on their potential applications in EMI shielding. PVA was selected due to its status as one of the few biodegradable organic polymers that exhibit favorable film-forming properties, non-toxicity, low cost, accessibility, and widespread use. The composite films were synthesized using a solution casting technique. Spectroscopic analyses indicated that the interactions between TiO 2 , GO, and PVA predominantly occur through hydrogen bonding. The incorporation of TiO 2  led to an increase in the crystallinity of the films. In composites containing GO, TiO 2  demonstrated an enhanced affinity for the polymer matrix, attributable to the hydrophilic characteristics of both components. This interaction had a significant impact on the EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) under transmission-line measurements, resulting in values of 3.27 dB/mm in the X-band and 7.28 dB/mm at 9.3 GHz. Conversely, the introduction of rGO yielded a diminished interaction with TiO 2 , which can be ascribed to its lower content of oxygen-containing functional groups. The higher electrical conductivity observed in rGO was the most prominent outcome. At a filler concentration of 1%, rGO exhibited a competitive effect, whereas at 4% filler concentration, a synergistic effect was observed. EMI SE values at 9.9 GHz were recorded at 31.34 dB mm −1  and 55.80 dB mm −1  for the respective filler concentrations, confirming that these PVA-based films function as shielding materials rather than simple radar-absorbing coatings. This investigation highlights that GO/TiO 2 /PVA and rGO/TiO 2 /PVA composite films possess exceptional EMI-shielding properties. The divergent interactions between GO and rGO with TiO 2  and PVA result in distinct EMI SE mechanisms, with rGO exhibiting superior performance.

Yuchang et al. [ 62 ] investigated the EMI-shielding properties of graphene nanosheets (GN) incorporated with BaTiO 3  ceramics. The composite material was fabricated through pressureless sintering, achieving a thickness of just 1.5 mm. Their findings demonstrated that both the real and imaginary components of the complex permittivity increased with higher GN content. The results regarding EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) indicated that the absorption mechanism was the primary contributor to the overall SE in the X-band, rather than reflection-dominant shielding. Notably, the total SE surpassed 40 dB in the X-band at a thickness of 1.5 mm, suggesting that GN/BaTiO 3  ceramics are excellent candidates for highly efficient, absorption-dominated EMI-shielding materials throughout the X-band.

Dinkaran et al .  [ 63 ] conducted a comprehensive study on polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) nanocomposites that demonstrate enhanced dielectric properties, microwave absorption capabilities, and EMI-shielding effectiveness. The research focused on composites incorporating NiO and NiO-embedded graphene hybrid nanostructures. The synthesis of NiO nanoparticles and NiO/graphene was achieved through hydrothermal reactions at a controlled temperature of 80 °C. The resultant nanocomposites were fabricated utilizing the solvent casting technique. Observations from scanning electron microscopy (SEM) indicated a homogeneous distribution of the NiO nanoparticles (at a concentration of 3%) throughout the PVDF matrix. The composites containing 10 wt% of NiO/Graphene/PVDF exhibited the highest conductivity of 6.8 × 10 −14  S m −1  at a frequency of 1000 Hz and a dielectric constant of 90. The incorporation of 3% NiO within the PVDF matrix led to a substantial enhancement in EMI shielding effectiveness (SE), achieving a maximum SE of 39 dB at a frequency of 10.3 GHz under transmission-line measurement conditions. This value is significantly higher than that of pristine PVDF and other tested samples, underscoring the potential of these nanocomposites for applications requiring robust electrical insulation and EMI shielding.

The integration of magnetic materials introduces magnetic dipoles that can interact with alternating electromagnetic fields. This interaction results in magnetic losses through processes such as natural resonance, exchange resonance, domain wall resonance, and eddy current effects. When these magnetic nanoparticles are embedded within graphene matrices, they enhance the mechanisms of dielectric and conductive losses, significantly broadening the frequency range of absorption. The remarkable electrical conductivity and extensive surface area of graphene facilitate the uniform anchoring of magnetic nanoparticles, thereby promoting robust interfacial coupling. This relationship aids in the attenuation of electromagnetic waves through various processes, including multiple-scattering, reflection–refraction cycles, and interfacial relaxation. Moreover, the hybridization of magnetic materials improves impedance matching by minimizing the mismatch between the impedance of free space and the intrinsic impedance of the shielding material. This enhancement is essential for achieving effective absorption-dominated EMI suppression.

The principal function of magnetic promoters in graphene-EMI-shielding nanocomposites is attributed to iron ( α -ferrite) or its oxides, including magnetite (Fe 3 O 4 ) and gamma-hematite ( γ -Fe 2 O 3 ). Additionally, this role may be fulfilled by mixed compounds, predominantly oxides, that incorporate other metals, such as cobalt ferrite (CoFe 2 O 4 ), nickel ferrite (NiFe 2 O 4 ), manganese–zinc (MnZn) ferrites, and barium hexaferrite (BaFe 12 O 19 ). Metallic forms of cobalt and nickel are also suitable for this application.

Bhaskaran et al. [ 64 ] studied the EMI shielding effectiveness of epoxy nanocomposites incorporating graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) and Fe 3 O 4  nanoparticles, collectively referred to as Fe 3 O 4 /GNP hybrids, within the X-band frequency range of 8–12.4 GHz. The hybrid nanostructures were synthesized in situ using a straightforward co-precipitation technique and subsequently integrated into the epoxy matrix through a solvent-free melt blending process. SEM analysis revealed a uniform distribution of Fe 3 O 4  nanoparticles on the GNP sheets. A series of epoxy nanocomposites with varying ratios of Fe 3 O 4 /GNP, GNP, and/or Fe 3 O 4  nanoparticles were synthesized and assessed for their EMI shielding effectiveness. Overall, the incorporation of Fe 3 O 4 /GNP hybrids resulted in enhanced EMI-shielding performance compared to samples containing only GNP or Fe 3 O 4  in equivalent amounts. In particular, a 1-mm-thick composite sample with a weight ratio of 3:1 (GNP:Fe 3 O 4 ) was able to attenuate 89% of the incident wave power in transmission, corresponding to an EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) of 9.6 dB in the X-band, with the remaining 11% transmitted through the shield.

Wang et al. [ 65 ] have reported on graphene-wrapped multiloculated NiFe 2 O 4  composites, which function as multifunctional electromagnetic absorbing and EMI-shielding materials. The overlapping flexible graphene creates conductive networks that enhance polarization properties and establish pathways for electron transmission, thereby optimizing the dielectric constant of the composites. Additionally, the incorporation of magnetic NiFe 2 O 4  introduces a synergistic magnetic-dielectric effect. The numerous non-homogeneous interfaces not only facilitate effective interfacial polarization but also, due to the carefully designed multiloculated structure of NiFe 2 O 4 , strengthen multi-scattering and multi-reflection sites. This design expands the transmission path for EM waves, enhancing overall performance. The findings indicate that optimal impedance matching occurs at a lower concentration of filler, achieving a peak reflection loss (RL) value of − 48.1 dB in the investigated frequency range, which corresponds to almost complete absorption at the matching frequency. Furthermore, increasing the concentration of fillers enhances green EMI shielding by absorption, where the dominant mechanism is EM wave dissipation within the absorber rather than reflection from the surface.

Manobalan et al. [ 66 ] reported the effects of filler content and concentration on the structural, electrical, mechanical, and EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) of hybrid composites composed of epoxy (Ep), graphene (G), and nickel ferrite (NiF). The research specifically emphasizes the role of nickel ferrite in achieving magnetic alignment under a low magnetic field of 0.165 T, as well as the subsequent impact of this alignment on the properties of the resulting composites. The graphene content was systematically varied within the Ep/G composite to determine the electrical threshold, which was identified to be 1 wt% through a straightforward solution-based processing technique. Moreover, the study explored the enhancement of dielectric and magnetic losses attributed to the incorporation of magnetic nanoparticles of NF. This examination was based on permittivity and permeability measurements conducted across a frequency range of 8.2 to 12.4 GHz.

Yin et al. [ 67 ] successfully synthesized Ni 0.5 Co 0.5 Fe 2 O 4 /graphene composites through a one-step hydrothermal method. The findings revealed that the addition of graphene significantly enhances the microwave absorption performance within an optimal range, with magnetic loss serving as the predominant mechanism contributing to the microwave absorption characteristics of the composites. The maximum reflection loss observed was − 30.92 dB at 0.84 GHz, with a − 10 dB absorption bandwidth of 0.58–1.19 GHz at a composite composition of 12 wt% graphene and a sample thickness of 4 mm, highlighting their performance as microwave absorbing layers in the low-frequency range.

Zhang et al. [ 68 ] reported the preparation of EMI-shielding nanocomposites utilizing a low filler content by incorporating magnetic nickel particles. The composite filler, consisting of graphene and nickel (GN), was synthesized through the in situ reduction of nickel ions in a basic ethanol–water solution. In this composite, the graphene layers were enhanced with flower-shaped nickel particles roughly 100 nm in size, and homogeneous films of the ternary composites were produced from polybenzoxazine and GN. The findings revealed that the addition of just 1 wt% of GN increased the electrical conductivity from 1.57 × 10 –12  S cm −1  (at 1 Hz) to 3.10 × 10 –4  S cm −1  (at 1 Hz). As a result, these composites demonstrated high EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) in the X-band range under standard waveguide measurements and exhibited an absorption-dominant mechanism, with 3 wt% of GN satisfying the typical ≥ 20 dB SE requirement for commercial enclosure-type shields. Additionally, the uniform dispersion of GN and the robust interaction between the fillers and the matrix led to significant enhancements in storage modulus, glass transition temperature, thermal stability, and thermal conductivity.

The concurrent incorporation of dielectric and magnetic components into graphene-based composites is among the most effective strategies for achieving absorption-dominated EMI shielding, in both radar-absorbing coatings (characterized by RL and absorption bandwidth) and enclosure-type shields (characterized by SE, SE A  and SE R ). By introducing dielectric materials such as BaTiO 3 , TiO 2,  and SiO 2 , the complex permittivity can be tuned, while magnetic materials such as Fe 3 O 4 , Ni, Co, and ferrites control the complex permeability, enabling optimized impedance matching and synergistic dielectric–magnetic loss mechanisms. As a result, these hybrid architectures exhibit multimodal energy dissipation (interfacial polarization, dipolar relaxation, magnetic resonance, and conductive losses), leading to high reflection loss minima and broad absorption bandwidths for radar-absorbing designs, and high shielding effectiveness for enclosure-type configurations, even at relatively small thicknesses.

Zhao et al. [ 69 ] developed amorphous TiO 2  and SiO 2 -coated Ni composite microspheres through a two-step method. The insulating SiO 2  shell enhances the antioxidation capabilities of the core–shell Ni–SiO 2  composite microspheres compared to pure Ni microspheres. Furthermore, these core–shell microspheres exhibit superior microwave absorption properties relative to both pure Ni microspheres and Ni–TiO 2  composites. For the Ni–SiO 2  composite microspheres, an optimal reflection loss (RL) of − 40.0 dB (corresponding to 99.99% absorption at the matching frequency) was recorded at 12.6 GHz with an absorber thickness of just 1.5 mm. The effective absorption bandwidth (defined as RL <  − 10 dB) can be adjusted from 3.1 to 14.4 GHz by varying the absorber thickness within the range of 1.5 to 4.5 mm, confirming their role as radar-absorbing fillers rather than enclosure-type shields. The outstanding microwave absorption capabilities of the Ni–SiO 2  composite microspheres are attributed to a higher attenuation constant, Debye relaxation, interface polarization of the core–shell structure, and the synergistic effects of high dielectric loss and high magnetic loss.

Guo et al. [ 70 ] successfully synthesized reduced graphene oxide (rGO) coated with barium titanate (BT) through a simple methodology. A comprehensive series of measurements were conducted to assess the morphology and structural properties of the composites. The rGO@BT/PVDF composites incorporating filler amounts of 10, 15, 20, and 25 wt%, demonstrated broad frequency bands ( R L  <  − 10 dB) with peak reflection coefficients of − 33.2, − 45.3, − 32.9, and − 22.8 dB, respectively, within 2–18 GHz at thicknesses of 1–5 mm, consistent with high-performance radar-absorbing layers. In addition to these absorber-type metrics, the authors also evaluated EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) in transmission and derived shielding effectiveness due to absorption (SE A ) and reflection (SE R ), thereby separating the contributions of absorption and reflection to overall shielding behavior. Additionally, the study detailed analyses of electrical conductivity and skin depth to facilitate further investigation.

Jin et al. [ 71 ] synthesized methyl vinyl silicone rubber (VMQ) nanocomposites through solution blending of VMQ with a hybrid comprising graphene nanoplatelets and Fe 3 O 4 @BaTiO 3  (GFBT), as well as multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs). The primary objective of this study was to enhance the EMI-shielding performance of VMQ. The GFBT hybrid was produced utilizing a two-step solvothermal method, with low-defect graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) acting as carriers for the Fe 3 O 4 @BaTiO 3  nanoparticles. Microscopy observation confirmed the successful incorporation of Fe 3 O 4  particles, approximately 200 nm in size, and BaTiO 3  nanoparticles, approximately 20 nm in size, onto the GNPs. Both the GFBT hybrid and MWCNTs exhibited good dispersion within the resultant VMQ/GFBT/MWCNTs (VGFBTM) nanocomposite. The composite revealed a total filler loading of 16.1 wt% (with a GFBT to MWCNT ratio of 5:1), yielding a shielding effectiveness (SE) ranging from 26.7 to 33.3 dB in the 1.0–20.0 GHz range, which corresponds to more than 99.8% attenuation of transmitted electromagnetic power in the tested configuration. The observed synergistic effect between the GFBT hybrid and MWCNTs significantly contributed to enhanced dielectric and magnetic losses, thereby improving the EMI shielding effectiveness of the VMQ matrix. Furthermore, the electrical conductivity of the VGFBTM nanocomposite was notably elevated compared to that of the pure VMQ, attributable to the formation of a conductive network structure facilitated by the two-dimensional GNPs and one-dimensional MWCNTs.

sections.heading: EMI measurement methodology and common pitfalls
paragraphs: Besides the research reports dedicated to the design and development of the most effective EMI-shielding materials, a lot of papers were also published on the EMI SE testing methodology, as well as common pitfalls. Usually, the experimental assessment of EMI-shielding performance for a specific structure mainly depends on its capacity to attenuate EMWs and the degree to which these incident waves are absorbed, reflected, or transmitted through the material. Real testing has shown that the shielding efficiency of a material is determined by several factors, and small changes in one aspect can affect other factors, resulting in differences in the overall shielding performance of the materials. A crucial element in determining the SE is the proximity of the shield to the radiation source. EMI measurements/tests are categorized as shown in Fig.  4 . Fig. 4 EMI measurement techniques

Practically, the electromagnetic radiation field can be divided into three regions depending on the distance ( r ) between the radiation source and the shield. These regions include the near-field and far-field regions, identified by  r  <  λ /2 π  and  r  >  λ /2 π , respectively, with the transition region ( r  ≈  λ /2 π ) situated in between. From a practical point of view, the near-field testing setup was more frequently used [ 72 ]. This setup has the main role in the assessment of EMW leakage from integrated circuits and their related equipment within the near-field range. Application of this method was important for maintaining the reliability and safety of the electronic devices, resulting in higher efficiency in the detection and mitigation of EMW leakages.

Based on theory, the techniques generally used to measure the EMI under two broad categories, such as emission testing and immunity testing, are presented in Fig.  4 . There are two types of emissions considered for EMI measurements, radiated emission and conducted emission. Radiated emission testing is done in the open-area test-site setup or in chambers such as anechoic chambers, GTEMs, or reverberation chambers. Conducted emission testing was done to measure the EMI generated due to an abrupt change in voltages and currents within the circuitry of the EUT. In order to do this, methods such as LISN, 1X method, probe method, or TEM cell method were used. All these EMI measurement methods were widely explained elaborately, and the relevant internationally accepted standards were developed. Generally, the standard radiated emission testing is done within the frequency band of 30 MHz–1 GHz (corresponding wavelengths are 10 m and 0.3 m, respectively). One of the most common methods for radiated emission testing for large instruments was performed at an open-area test-site (OATS). This type of setup usually consists of a theoretically infinite metallic ground plane, a receiving antenna connected to an EMI receiver or spectrum analyzer via cables, and the EUT, usually kept at a distance of 3 m or 10 m (unless specified differently) from the receiver. The distance is measured from the nearest outer surface of the EUT to the receiver antenna. Such a large distance between the EUT and the receiver is primarily chosen to make certain that the measurements are taken in the far-field region, where the radiated field is more stable as compared to that in the near-field or Fresnel region. To release the analysis of the EMI SE in both near-field and far-field regions, a shielded chamber and a network analyzer (NA) method were developed. The basic NA equipment contains two primary types: the scalar network analyzer (SNA) and the vector network analyzer (VNA). The SNA was used for testing the amplitude of electrical signals, and it was unable to measure more complex parameters like permittivity and permeability. Recently, researchers have adopted the VNA for measuring the EMI SE of various materials and structures. This method offers simple and straightforward calibration, making it a preferred method among researchers. Generally, VNAs were able to transmit, receive, and dynamically record EMI intensities over a wide range of the frequency spectrum. The most widely used  methods for measuring EMI shielding effectiveness utilize transmission/reflection line configurations, incorporating coaxial cables and waveguide techniques. Additionally,   free-space setups are employed, including   anechoic chambers, Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) systems, and specialized reflectivity measurement tools [ 73 ]. Another group of methods used to reduce the EMI was based on the application of electromagnetic shields, EMI filters, changes in the circuit topology itself, and the spread spectrum technique. Special attention was given to the electromagnetic shielding since it is one of the most preferred EMI reduction techniques. Various methods employed to measure the shielding effectiveness of materials were well described theoretically as well as mathematically.

According to the published literature data, one of the present misconceptions in EMI SE studies is the belief that if SEA > SER, or if the SEA to SER ratio exceeds 1, the shielding mechanism is dominated by the absorption. This perspective fundamentally misrepresents the interpretation of shielding mechanisms when relying on ratios of SE parameters. In fact, the SEA indicates the proportion of the EMW penetrating the shield (accounting for reflected waves deducted from the incident waves) in relation to the T. It does not directly demonstrate the ratio between the incident and the reflected or transmitted EMWs. Another misunderstanding is to correlate the shielding coefficients to evaluate a material’s dominant shielding mechanisms. As a result, if R surpasses A for a given shield, the shielding mechanism is dominated by reflection. This was interpreted as if R exceeded 0.5 or the SER surpassed 3 dB. Common mistakes related to misinterpreting EMI-shielding metrics include (a) assuming a high SEA/SER ratio automatically equates to absorption dominance, (b) overestimating a material’s effectiveness based solely on its intrinsic conductivity, ignoring the critical need for optimized impedance matching, and (c) miscalculating the required thickness or filler content necessary to achieve targeted absorption rates. To avoid these pitfalls, users and businesses must use precise testing protocols and analytical methods when evaluating EMI-shielding materials. It is critical to assess both reflectance and absorbance independently and ensure impedance matching is optimized, providing true absorption-dominant performance. Another pitfall was regarding the safety risks of traditional reflection-dominant EMI Shields. Usually, when businesses select EMI-shielding materials, the priority often leans toward materials exhibiting high conductivity. In fact, while highly conductive metals and materials like MXenes and graphene promise strong shielding, their predominantly reflective mechanism poses hidden risks. Instead of fully absorbing electromagnetic waves, these materials primarily reflect them, inadvertently generating secondary electromagnetic pollution. Such secondary radiation can disrupt nearby sensitive equipment in critical sectors, including medical devices, aerospace instrumentation, and military communications systems. The risks associated with reflection-dominant EMI shields can include (a) unintentional interference with medical devices, potentially causing erroneous readings or equipment malfunction, (b) disruption of sensitive military or aerospace electronic systems, compromising mission safety and reliability, and (c) increased legal liabilities and regulatory compliance challenges due to secondary radiation interference. In order to ensure safety and reliability, users and businesses must select materials and structural designs that prioritize electromagnetic wave absorption. Opting for absorption-dominant shielding reduces secondary radiation and prevents harmful interference, thus safeguarding both end-users and brand reputation.

Another very important pitfall is related to the prioritization of material choice without giving due attention to structural design. Maybe it is logical to select an EMI-shielding material solely based on intrinsic properties, such as high electrical conductivity, but neglecting thoughtful structural design can undermine overall shielding performance. Even advanced materials like MXenes and conductive polymers could reflect the electromagnetic waves rather than absorb them. So, the main key risks related to structural design oversight include (a) development of reflection-dominant shields that fail to reduce secondary electromagnetic pollution, (b) suboptimal shielding performance, requiring costly redesigns or additional layers for correction, and (c) compromised structural integrity or mechanical performance due to inadequate attention to structural detail. To address these issues, businesses must integrate material selection with deliberate structural design considerations.

sections.heading: Graphene-based EMI-shielding materials on the market
paragraphs: Up to today, commercially available EMI-shielding materials and products have been based on metal. However, a significant quantum of research work and results demonstrate that carbon nanostructure-based nanocomposite materials can change conventional metal shielding, especially graphene’s excellent conductivity, making its nanocomposites a perfect candidate for EMI-shielding applications [ 74 ]. Thus, the need for materials that can protect people but also instruments from both EWs and interference is increasing along with technological development. A material with EMI-shielding efficiency of 20 dB is appropriate for commercial applications.

Graphenest and Lohmann GmbH, a developer of adhesive technologies, have announced the signing of a joint-venture agreement to co-develop next-generation graphene-based adhesive systems for EMI shielding and thermal management applications. Recently, research teams from the University of Calgary, University of British Columbia, University of Waterloo, and Aalto University have developed an all-graphene water-based ink for 3D printing via direct ink writing. This ink could unlock new possibilities for addressing environmental challenges, such as eliminating invisible electromagnetic pollution from our surroundings. The eco-friendly graphene ink enables applications in various fields, including electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding, electronics, and environmental protection, while providing a scalable solution for next-generation 3D-printed technologies. Hydro Graph Clean Power has announced successful testing of its flagship product, FGA-1, fractal graphene, in electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding. The integration of HydroGraph’s graphene in epoxy resin was reported to achieve substantial EMI-shielding properties by reaching an 80 dB attenuation (a reduction of signal strength during transmission) in shielded enclosures of less than 1 mm thick. Minimum ratings for consumer protection are 30 dB and range from 60 to 80 dB for automotive and aerospace applications. Hydro Graph Clean Power has announced its collaboration with Kansas-based EMP Shield Inc., a company focused on protecting devices from destructive electromagnetic interference. Under this collaboration, the HydroGraph and EMP Shield are developing advanced electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding using HydroGraph’s high-purity graphene. Electronic equipment can be protected from EMI by conductive or absorptive materials and coatings. HydroGraph and EMP shield are working together to develop coatings and insulated barriers to protect electronic devices by blocking unwanted disruptions or transmission of electronic data. UK-based graft polymer has joined a consortium led by the Vinca Institute of Nuclear Sciences relating to the GrinShield Project Twinning program for new graphene-based composites in electromagnetic interference shielding. The initiative, supported by French, German, and Slovenian teams, was formed in response to the growing demand for materials that can mitigate the effects of electromagnetic waves (EWs). RTP Company has developed a family of thermoplastic compounds that improve the performance of electronic devices for use with the new Bluetooth™ wireless communications protocol. These custom materials feature modified electrical and dielectric properties that enhance signal transmission and reception. A complementary product line provides important EMI shielding to help meet FCC regulations.

sections.heading: Challenges, trade-offs, and future directions
paragraphs: In practical deployment, graphene-based EMI-shielding materials must balance several competing requirements, including processability, electrical conductivity, mechanical integrity, scalability, and cost. High loadings of graphene or hybrid conductive/magnetic fillers generally improve conductivity and SE but quickly degrade melt or solution processability, increase viscosity, and embrittle the matrix, compromising toughness and flexibility. Achieving ultra-high conductivity through high-quality graphene, MXenes, or metal particles often requires complex, multistep processing (e.g., vacuum filtration, CVD growth, freeze-drying of aerogels), which is difficult to scale industrially and raises manufacturing cost. By contrast, highly processable, low-cost routes such as conventional melt compounding or solution casting are more scalable but usually demand higher filler contents to reach comparable SE, again negatively impacting mechanical performance and density. Absorption-dominant designs with engineered porosity or hierarchical architectures can reduce secondary EM pollution but introduce additional processing steps and potential mechanical weakening, which must be weighed against safety and regulatory drivers. A critical design challenge, therefore, is to optimize microstructure and filler architecture so that acceptable SE or RL targets are met with minimal filler loading and processing complexity, maintaining mechanical robustness while keeping material and manufacturing costs within application-specific constraints [ 75 ,  76 ,  77 – 78 ].

To successfully advance from lab-scale prototypes to viable industrial applications, a series of critical translational barriers must be systematically navigated. A primary bottleneck is manufacturing scalability and large-scale production. While premium bench-scale synthesis routes like liquid-phase exfoliation yield high-quality graphene sheets, scaling these processes up to industrial metric tons routinely introduces structural defects, inconsistent layer counts, and poor batch-to-batch reproducibility. These structural inconsistencies directly increase cost barriers, as pristine graphene architectures remain prohibitively expensive compared to conventional carbon materials like carbon black, heavily limiting their integration into mass-market consumer electronics unless low-cost pathways can be fully optimized. Furthermore, serious environmental impacts and recyclability concerns stem from the fact that functionalized derivatives often rely on aggressive oxidizing acids and toxic reducing agents, while thermoset matrices form rigid, cross-linked structures that present significant landfill and disposal challenges. Transitioning to green reducing agents and bio-based, recyclable thermoplastic matrices is therefore a vital future direction. This must be accompanied by comprehensive long-term durability evaluations. Nanocomposites deployed in demanding sectors like aerospace or automotive electronics must endure accelerated thermal, mechanical, and environmental aging to guarantee that the embedded conductive networks do not degrade, delaminate, or experience physical fatigue over extended operational life cycles.

Concurrently, evaluating the true industrial potential of these materials remains severely limited by a historical lack of unified benchmarking metrics across the literature, where papers typically present standalone, absolute electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness (EMI SE) values evaluated at completely arbitrary material thicknesses. To accurately distinguish the highest-performing material configurations, future research must shift toward normalized performance comparisons, utilizing unified evaluation parameters such as Specific EMI SE (which divides the total shielding effectiveness by both the material thickness and mass density) to look past raw values and balance structural characteristics against weight penalties. Ideally, this cross-system benchmarking should be visualized using multi-variable statistical comparisons and Ashby-style performance maps that plot specific EMI SE against crucial structural trade-off fields like tensile strength, electrical conductivity, or material costs. By establishing these unified evaluation frameworks, the academic community can transparently map the performance limits of distinct thermoplastic, thermoset, and foam matrices, providing a clear engineering roadmap that bridges the gap between fundamental research and practical real-world adoption.

Our review does not aim to provide a comprehensive summary of recent progress in EMI-shielding materials, as the field continues to publish new and clever designs with improved performance. Several good reviews have already provided different perspectives on related topics of effective EMI-shielding materials. In this review, we highlight several typical graphene–polymer nanocomposite systems based on different polymer types, their advancements, and trends in recent years. The current trends in the EMI field are to design and produce high-efficiency, lightweight, thinner-and-stronger, and broadband electromagnetic shielding materials. To reach this goal, different approaches can be attempted. Among the possible limitations, the achievement of uniform dispersion of graphene within a thermoplastic is non-trivial. Graphene tends to aggregate due to strong van der Waals forces and hydrophobicity, impeding the formation of an optimal network at low filler loadings. Functionalization of graphene or using compatibilizers may help, but such treatments can compromise conductivity. Then, to achieve high shielding, high filler loadings may be necessary, which can adversely affect processability, mechanical integrity, flexibility, or transparency and increase the material cost of the thermoplastic composite. Thus, designing architectures (e.g., oriented, layered, foam) that reduce filler loading while maintaining shielding is key. For practical applications, minimal material thickness and weight are preferred. While some thermoplastic graphene composites have achieved high SE values, many required significant thickness. The move toward ultra-thin and ultra-light shields is ongoing. In many early systems, reflection dominates shielding, which may cause secondary electromagnetic pollution. Shifting toward absorption-dominant designs (e.g., via foam structures, magnetic fillers combined with graphene) is a forward trend. Large-scale production of graphene with consistent quality and the cost of incorporating it into thermoplastics at an industrial-scale remain issues. Moreover, reproducibility and long-term stability (thermal, mechanical, and environmental) need further demonstration. Combining graphene with other conductive or magnetic fillers (e.g., carbon nanotubes, metal nanoparticles, ferrites) can lead to synergetic performance improvements. For instance, the multilayer TPU/graphite/ferrite study (G/F/G stacking) achieved ~ 54 dB SE [ 15 ]. Foam or microcellular composites, oriented fiber networks, layered laminates, and additive manufacturing approaches are all promising. For example, the TPU/GNP microcellular foam achieved good performance at low filler loading. Graphene not only contributes to EMI shielding but may also enhance thermal conductivity and mechanical robustness. Some studies (e.g., PP@G) show high thermal conductivity (~ 87 W m −1  K −1 ) alongside high EMI SE (~ 88 dB) [ 18 ].
